title: The spirit
hookLine: they ask about the spirit; say it is of my Lord's command, and you were given little knowledge (17:85)

cards: What are you, exactly? Not your name, not your job. The thing that is awake behind your eyes right now, hearing these words.
Philosophers have written libraries about it. Neuroscientists study the brain every day and still argue over how it gives rise to a single moment of experience; some call it the hard problem.
Today, someone puts that question to a prophet, and the answer begins with silence.

teach.b: Bukhari records the scene from the companion Ibn Mas'ud.
He was walking with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through farmland in Medina, the Prophet leaning on a palm stalk, when some of the Jews of Medina asked him about the spirit. He went quiet.
Ibn Mas'ud realized revelation was coming and stood back.

Then the Prophet recited, in Pickthall's words: "They are asking thee concerning the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is by command of my Lord, and of knowledge ye have been vouchsafed but little." The word is ruh.
Its root, r-w-h, is shared with rih, wind, and rawh, ease, relief: something moving and unseen.
The Qur'an uses ruh for what God breathed into Adam, for the angel Jibril, called the trustworthy spirit, and in one verse for revelation itself. Which is meant here?
Many scholars said the human soul; others said Jibril, or the Qur'an. The verse doesn't settle it.
It answers with amr, command: the spirit belongs to the order of God's command, the word Be.

teach.h: OF KNOWLEDGE YE HAVE BEEN VOUCHSAFED BUT LITTLE.
teach.b: Then it turns to every reader: you have been given only a little knowledge. Not none. A little.
That's no insult to curiosity; Muslim scholars went on to write whole books about the soul, knowing the edge of the map was drawn here. And there's honesty in it.
A prophet, asked the deepest question, doesn't make up an answer. He waits, and the answer includes the words: you know little.

how: Muslim scholars have written at length about the ruh, while citing 17:85 as a reminder that its reality belongs to God's command; many teachers use the verse to model humility in answering hard questions.

o: the spirit, which belongs to God's command
a strong desert wind that brings rain
the brain, and the thoughts it produces

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: the verse gives a full description of the soul
it says the spirit is of God's command, and that people have been given only a little knowledge.
scholars agree ruh in 17:85 means the human soul
many said the soul; others said Jibril or the Qur'an.
ruh shares a root with the Arabic for wind
r-w-h gives ruh, rih (wind) and rawh (ease, relief).

games.q: you're walking through farmland and someone asks you the deepest question there is: what is the spirit? what does the Prophet do, in Bukhari's report?
o: answer at once from what he already knew.
go quiet, and wait for revelation.
games.why: he went quiet; Ibn Mas'ud stood back; then he recited 17:85, which says people have been given only a little knowledge.

practice: Close your eyes and notice that you're aware: of sound, of the weight of your body, of this voice.
Now look, gently, for the one who's aware; you may find thoughts and sensations but not the thing itself, so rest in the question the way the verse does. If you pray, you can end with subhan Allah.

wordCard.voice: Ruh. The spirit, from a root of wind and relief: of the command of God, and beyond the little knowledge we're given. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the spirit, from the root r-w-h, shared with rih, wind.

carryVoice: Your line: a little knowledge. Not none, a little, and honest about the rest. Until tomorrow.
